## Cards

### 01 · Food without a rulebook
Group: **Day to day** · Referral chip: **Ask a dietitian** · Products shown: *none*

- Canadian guidelines describe several styles of eating that work well with diabetes, including Mediterranean, Nordic, DASH and vegetarian ✎ `1.1`
- Canada’s food guide suggests plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with protein from plants more often `1.2`
- Make water your drink of choice `1.3`
- Choose whole and less processed foods more often than sugary drinks, fast food and refined grains `1.4`
- Notice when you’re hungry and when you’re full `1.5`
- Culture and food traditions can be part of healthy eating `1.6`

> **Note** `1.note` — A registered dietitian can help you make a meal plan that fits your culture, your tastes and your blood sugar goals.

*Sources for this card:* Nutrition Therapy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Healthy eating recommendations (Health Canada); Basic carbohydrate counting for diabetes management (07/25) (Diabetes Canada)

### 02 · Carb counting
Group: **Day to day** · Referral chip: **Ask a dietitian** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `portions` — Meal Measure Unit (4382)

- Canadian guidelines suggest learning to count carbohydrate, because how much you eat at one time usually matters ✎ `2.1`
- Your body turns carbohydrate into sugar, which raises your blood sugar. Both the kind and the amount matter `2.2`
- Carbohydrate is in grains and starches, fruit, some vegetables, legumes, milk and milk alternatives, sweet foods and many prepared foods. Meat and alternatives, most vegetables and fats have little `2.3`
- A common guide for most people is about 45 to 60 g of carbohydrate at a meal and 15 to 30 g at a snack. A dietitian or diabetes educator can help you set your own goals ✎ `2.4`
- Try to keep each meal and snack within 5 g of your goal `2.5`
- On a Nutrition Facts table, check the serving size first. Then take the total carbohydrate and subtract the fibre: 36 g of carbohydrate with 6 g of fibre counts as 30 g `2.6`

> **Note** `2.note` — If you take insulin with meals, work out with your team how carbohydrate and insulin fit together. This card covers counting only.

*Sources for this card:* Nutrition Therapy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Basic carbohydrate counting for diabetes management (07/25) (Diabetes Canada)

### 03 · Moving your body
Group: **Day to day** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `moving` — Dex4 Key Chain (4731), FlipBelt Diabetes Supply Carrying Case (4529)

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Aim for at least 150 minutes a week of activity that raises your breathing and heart rate, like brisk walking, cycling, swimming or dancing `3.1`
- Spread it over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 days in a row off `3.2`
- Start slowly, with 5 to 10 minutes a day, and build up. Less than 150 minutes still has benefits `3.3`
- Add strength exercises at least 2 times a week, with weights, bands or your own body weight. If you’re new to them, get some instruction first `3.4`
- Break up long periods of sitting. Canadian guidelines suggest getting up briefly every 20 to 30 minutes ✎ `3.5`
- If you’ve been inactive for a while, talk to your doctor before starting anything harder than a brisk walk. If you have chest pain, pressure or discomfort, or you’re much more short of breath than usual, stop the activity and call 911 right away. These can be signs of a heart attack. Tell your doctor about it too, before you exercise again ✎ `3.6`
- Exercise can lower your blood sugar for up to 48 hours. If you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar, check regularly and carry fast-acting sugar. More in Staying Safe, under Lows that sneak up `3.7`

> **Note** `3.note` — Ask your team how to plan food and medicines around activity, especially if you use insulin.

*Sources for this card:* Physical Activity and Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Exercise & Activity (Diabetes Canada); Signs of a heart attack (Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada)

### 04 · Alcohol and cannabis
Group: **Day to day** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Canadian guidelines (2023) say that if you don’t drink, it’s healthier not to start. If you do drink, talk with your team about what’s right for you ✎ `4.1`
- Don’t drink if you’re pregnant or trying to get pregnant, breastfeeding, have a personal or family history of drinking problems, are about to drive or do anything that needs your full attention, or take certain medicines. Ask your pharmacist about yours. The 2018 sheet in this card’s Sources gives drink limits that are older than the 2023 advice on this card ✎ `4.2`
- If you take insulin or some other diabetes medicines, a low can come up to 24 hours after drinking. Eat carbohydrate when you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and make sure someone with you knows how to help, including calling 911 if you pass out. More in Staying Safe, under Lows that sneak up `4.3`
- Alternating alcoholic drinks with water helps you avoid getting dehydrated `4.4`
- Canadian guidelines (2023) say that if you drink, cutting down lowers the risk to your health, and that this may mean no more than 2 standard drinks a week. At 2 standard drinks or fewer a week you’re likely to avoid harm from alcohol, more than 2 at one time raises the risk of harms such as injuries, and less is better. Your team can help if you want to cut down ✎ `4.5`
- Recreational cannabis isn’t recommended for teens or adults with diabetes. With type 1, avoid it, because it raises the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) ✎ `4.6`
- If you do use cannabis, edibles can contain carbohydrate, and cannabis can make you hungrier. Adults who use it should be offered advice on lowering the risks ✎ `4.7`

> **Note** `4.note` — Alcohol and cannabis aren’t things to hide from your team. Your health-care providers should talk about them with you regularly, without judgement. ✎

*Sources for this card:* Alcohol and diabetes (04/18) (Diabetes Canada); Diabetes and Drinking (Diabetes Canada); Mental Health and Diabetes: 2023 Update (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Canada's Guidance on Alcohol and Health (2023) (Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction); Cannabis Use in Adults and Adolescents with Diabetes (Diabetes Canada)

### 05 · Distress, stress and sleep
Group: **Day to day** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Living with diabetes can feel like a burden. Its constant demands can lead to diabetes distress, low moods and anxiety ✎ `5.1`
- You may feel angry, guilty, frightened, discouraged or low. These are valid responses to a long-term condition ✎ `5.2`
- Depression is more common in people with diabetes, and there are effective treatments `5.3`
- Problems with eating, sleeping and stress are common too. Tell your team about them `5.4`
- So is fear of lows. If it’s holding you back, tell your team, because there are ways to help `5.5`
- Canadian guidelines say everyone with diabetes, and parents and caregivers of young people with diabetes, should be checked regularly for diabetes distress. Your team may give you a short questionnaire to fill in before a visit ✎ `5.6`
- Regular activity can lower stress and help you relax and sleep `5.7`

> **Note** `5.note` — If it isn’t easing, or you’re struggling to get through the day, tell your diabetes team or your doctor rather than waiting it out.

*Sources for this card:* Taking care of your mental health (Diabetes Canada); Mental Health and Diabetes: 2023 Update (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Exercise & Activity (Diabetes Canada); Mental Health Support (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); 9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (Canada))

*Visual figure: crisis, routes.*

*New labels this figure adds:*

- If you’re thinking about harming yourself, call or text 9-8-8, Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline, any time of day or night. If your safety is at risk right now, call 911. `5.fig.body`
- If it isn’t easing, or you’re struggling to get through the day `5.fig.routes.1.prompt`
- Tell your diabetes team `5.fig.routes.1.chips.1`

### 06 · Flying with diabetes supplies
Group: **Day to day** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `flying` — Frio Insulin Cooling Wallet Small (4844), Pen Plus Diabetic Travel Case (4255), Sharps Container 1L (4350)

- Keep insulin and your supplies in your carry-on. Don’t put insulin in checked luggage, because temperature changes can damage it ✎ `6.1`
- Insulin, and juice or gel to treat a low, can go through security in amounts over 100 mL. Declare them to the screening officer separately `6.2`
- Syringes are allowed with the needle guard on, as long as you’re carrying the medicine they’re for `6.3`
- Pumps and sensors are allowed. Don’t wear them through the body scanner or put a pump through the X-ray machine. You can ask for a physical search instead, in private if you like ✎ `6.4`
- You don’t have to tell screening staff you have diabetes, and you don’t have to take off your pump. Just tell the screening officer you’re wearing one `6.5`
- Keep medicine in its labelled packaging. Bring a letter from your doctor and a list of your medicines from your pharmacist ✎ `6.6`
- Pack spare insulin and supplies. In the heat, keep insulin in an insulated bag. In the cold, keep it close to your body so it doesn’t freeze `6.7`

> **Note** `6.note` — Crossing time zones can change when you take insulin or diabetes pills. Plan it with your doctor or diabetes educator before you go.

*Sources for this card:* Diabetic supplies (Canadian Air Transport Security Authority); Air Travel (Diabetes Canada)

### 07 · Driving
Group: **Day to day** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- These steps are for people who take insulin, or a diabetes pill that can cause lows `7.1`
- Check your blood sugar right before you drive, any time you feel low, and at least every 4 hours while driving, or wear a real-time sensor ✎ `7.2`
- Don’t start driving if your blood sugar is below 4.0 mmol/L `7.3`
- After treating a low, wait at least 40 minutes, and until your blood sugar is at least 5.0 mmol/L, before you drive `7.4`
- If a low starts while you’re driving, stop somewhere safe, take the keys out of the ignition and treat it. The 40-minute wait applies here too `7.5`
- Keep fast-acting sugar within reach of the driver’s seat, and your meter and supplies with you `7.6`
- If you no longer feel the early signs of a low, or you’ve had a severe low in the past year, Canadian guidelines say to check right before you drive and at least every 2 hours while driving, or wear a real-time sensor ✎ `7.7`
- A severe low is one where you pass out or need someone else’s help. If you have one while driving, stop driving right away. Tell your health-care provider and your driver licensing office right away, and do the same if you have more than one severe low while awake in the past 6 months (12 months for commercial drivers). Your provider may tell you not to drive ✎ `7.8`
- You have the right to be assessed for a driver’s licence as an individual. Licensing is handled by each province and territory. Licensing offices require a higher level of medical fitness to drive a bus, a commercial van, a transport truck or an emergency vehicle. Canadian guidelines say commercial drivers should have a medical exam when they apply for their licence ✎ `7.9`

> **Note** `7.note` — Most Canadian guidance uses 3.9 for a low, and 4.0 for driving. This card uses 4.0 because the driving guidance does. If your team gave you a number, use theirs. ✎ *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Diabetes and Driving (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Drive Safe with Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Driving and Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 08 · Your feet, every day
Group: **Protecting your body** · Referral chip: **Ask your doctor** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `feet` — Infracare Socks (5040)

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Diabetes can damage the nerves and blood flow in your feet, so you may not feel a blister or cut, and it can be slower to heal `8.1`
- Wash your feet in warm, not hot, water and dry them well, especially between the toes `8.2`
- Check your feet and between your toes for cuts, blisters or changes. Use a hand mirror for the soles, or ask someone to help `8.3`
- Put lotion on your heels and soles, but not between your toes. Trim your nails straight across, not too short `8.4`
- Wear clean socks and well-fitting shoes. Test bath water with your hand before you step in `8.5`
- Have your bare feet checked by your doctor or a foot-care specialist, such as a podiatrist, chiropodist or foot-care nurse. Ask them to check for nerve damage and blood flow too `8.6`
- See your doctor or a foot-care specialist right away for swelling, warmth, redness or pain in your feet or legs, or for corns, calluses, ingrown toenails, warts or slivers. Don’t treat these yourself. An open sore (a foot ulcer) or signs of infection need care right away, even if they don’t hurt. Don’t wait if a sore gets more painful, red, warm, smelly or starts to drain, if your foot is red, warm and changing shape, or if skin turns black or your legs or feet hurt at rest: see your doctor right away or go to the emergency department. A serious foot infection doesn’t always cause a fever ✎ `8.7`
- Don’t go barefoot, even indoors. Don’t use over-the-counter corn or wart treatments, or put hot water bottles or heating pads on your feet `8.8`

> **Note** `8.note` — If you’ve been told your feet are at high risk, you may need checks more often, and shoes fitted by a professional.

*Sources for this card:* Foot care: a step toward good health (08/25) (Diabetes Canada); Foot Care (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetic Foot Ulcers (Wounds Canada); Diabetic Foot Complications: When is it an Emergency? (Wounds Canada (Canadian Association of Wound Care); in French, Plaies Canada)

### 09 · Your eyes
Group: **Protecting your body** · Referral chip: **Ask your optometrist or ophthalmologist** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Diabetes can damage the small blood vessels in the retina, at the back of the eye. This is called diabetic retinopathy `9.1`
- It often goes unnoticed until it affects your sight, so regular exams matter even when you see well `9.2`
- An optometrist or ophthalmologist does the exam, often after drops that widen your pupils `9.3`
- Have an eye exam once a year, unless your optometrist or ophthalmologist suggests something different. With type 2, the first exam is at diagnosis. With type 1, yearly exams start 5 years after diagnosis, from age 15. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team ✎ `9.4`
- Canadian eye specialists also suggest an exam at least once a year. If you’re planning a pregnancy, Canadian advice differs: the diabetes guidelines say to have an exam before you get pregnant and while you’re pregnant, and eye specialists suggest one in the first trimester ✎ `9.5`
- See an eye doctor right away if you notice dark spots, blurred, distorted or double vision, or large floaters. If you suddenly see flashes of light with a lot of new floaters, or part of your vision goes dark, don’t wait: see an eye doctor right away, or go to the emergency department if you can’t be seen today. It can be a sign of a torn or detached retina ✎ `9.6`
- Found early, retinopathy can often be treated successfully, and treatment can keep your sight from getting worse. Sight that has already been lost can’t be restored, which is why early exams matter `9.7`
- Keeping your blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in range helps protect your eyes `9.8`

> **Note** `9.note` — If an exam finds little or no damage, Canadian guidelines allow 1 to 2 years between exams with type 2. Your eye-care professional and diabetes team decide your schedule, and can share your results with each other. ✎

*Sources for this card:* Eye Damage (Diabetic Retinopathy) (Diabetes Canada); Retinopathy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetic Retinopathy | See The Possibilities (Canadian Ophthalmological Society); Diabetic Retinopathy (CNIB); Floaters and Flashing Lights (CNIB (content © Canadian Ophthalmological Society))

### 10 · Your kidneys
Group: **Protecting your body** · Referral chip: **Ask your doctor** · Products shown: *none*

- Diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease in Canada. Up to half of people with diabetes will have signs of kidney damage in their lifetime `10.1`
- Good diabetes management and regular screening can prevent or delay the loss of kidney function `10.2`
- Most people have no symptoms early on, so screening is how kidney disease is found `10.3`
- Screening is two tests: a urine test (ACR) that looks for protein, and a blood test (eGFR) that shows how well your kidneys are working `10.4`
- With type 2, screening starts at diagnosis. With type 1, it starts 5 years after diagnosis. After that, it’s once a year `10.5`
- Keeping your blood sugar and blood pressure at target, not smoking, and taking your medicines as prescribed all help protect your kidneys `10.6`
- If you have kidney disease, a dietitian can tell you whether to change how much protein, potassium, phosphate or salt you eat `10.7`
- Some diabetes medicines also help protect the kidneys and heart. Ask your team whether yours does, and don’t change a medicine on your own `10.8`

> **Note** `10.note` — Ask your team for your ACR and eGFR results, and what they mean for you. Children follow their own schedule, so ask your child’s team.

*Sources for this card:* Kidney Disease (Diabetes Canada); Chronic Kidney Disease in Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); End Diabetic Kidney Disease (Kidney Foundation of Canada)

### 11 · Your heart: the ABCDEs
Group: **Protecting your body** · Referral chip: **Ask your doctor** · Products shown: *none*

- Diabetes raises the risk of heart disease and stroke. Heart disease may come 15 years earlier than in people without diabetes `11.1`
- You can lower that risk considerably by working on all your risk factors with your team. They’re often summed up as the ABCDEs ✎ `11.2`
- A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over time. Most people aim for 7% or less `11.3`
- Most people aim for a blood pressure below 130/80 `11.4`
- The usual LDL (“bad”) cholesterol target is below 2.0 mmol/L `11.5`
- Some medicines protect the heart. Ask your team whether any are right for you `11.6`
- Regular physical activity and healthy eating `11.7`
- Screening for complications in your heart, feet, kidneys and eyes; stopping smoking, with help if you want it; and self-management, including handling stress `11.8`
- Have your blood pressure checked at every diabetes visit, your A1C every 3 months, and your cholesterol every year, or more often if you take medicine to lower it ✎ `11.9`

> **Note** `11.note` — Your targets are yours to set with your team. A1C targets are different in pregnancy, for older adults and for children 12 and under. ✎

*Sources for this card:* Heart Disease & Stroke (Diabetes Canada)

- C · Cholesterol `11.fig.columns.3.heading`

### 12 · Work and your rights
Group: **Protecting your body** · Referral chip: *none — orientation card* · Products shown: *none*

- People with diabetes should be eligible for any job they’re qualified for ✎ `12.1`
- People with diabetes should have the right to look after their diabetes in public places ✎ `12.2`
- People with diabetes have the right to care that supports the best quality of life wherever they are, including in hospital and long-term care ✎ `12.3`
- For a driver’s licence, you have the right to be assessed as an individual. More in Driving `12.4`
- Coverage for medicines, supplies and devices varies across Canada, and you may be eligible for the Disability Tax Credit `12.5`
- Diabetes Canada’s information and support line is 1-800-226-8464 `12.6`

> **Note** `12.note` — Position statements on employment, insurance and self-care in public places are linked from the rights page in this card’s Sources. ✎

*Sources for this card:* The Rights of People Living with Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Driving and Diabetes (Diabetes Canada)

## Referral band

*Sources for the band:* Eye Damage (Diabetic Retinopathy) (Diabetes Canada); Retinopathy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Chronic Kidney Disease in Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Kidney Disease (Diabetes Canada); Foot care: a step toward good health (08/25) (Diabetes Canada); Foot Care (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Heart Disease & Stroke (Diabetes Canada); Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

**Your checkup year** `band.heading`

- **Eyes** `band.1` — Once a year, unless your eye-care professional suggests something different. Type 2: the first exam at diagnosis. Type 1: from age 15, starting 5 years after diagnosis. For a child under 15, ask your child’s team. See Your eyes. ✎
  - *Where card 9's title appears in this body, it links to card 9.*
- **Kidneys** `band.2` — A urine test (ACR) and a blood test (eGFR) once a year: from diagnosis with type 2, and from 5 years after diagnosis with type 1. See Your kidneys.
  - *Where card 10's title appears in this body, it links to card 10.*
- **Feet** `band.3` — A bare-foot check by your doctor or a foot-care specialist at least once a year, including nerves and blood flow, and more often if you’re at high risk. In between, check them yourself every day: see Your feet, every day.
  - *Where card 8's title appears in this body, it links to card 8.*
- **Heart** `band.4` — Blood pressure at every diabetes visit, A1C about every 3 months or as your team advises, and cholesterol once a year. See Your heart: the ABCDEs.
  - *Where card 11's title appears in this body, it links to card 11.*

## Resources shelf

**Where to find more help** `shelf.heading`

### Mental health and support `shelf.1`

- **9-8-8: call or text, any time** — 9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline `shelf.1.1`  
  If you are thinking about suicide, or worried about someone who is. Free, 24/7, in English and French. If your safety is at risk, call 911.  
  <https://988.ca/> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* 9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (9-8-8: Suicide Crisis Helpline (Canada))
- **Taking care of your mental health** — Diabetes Canada `shelf.1.2`  
  Diabetes distress, low moods and anxiety, and when to reach out to your health-care team.  
  <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/life-with-diabetes/mental-health-and-diabetes/taking-care-of-your-mental-health> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* Taking care of your mental health (Diabetes Canada)
- **Mental health support** — Breakthrough T1D Canada `shelf.1.3`  
  A directory with information about registered mental health providers, and a guide for parents and caregivers of children and teens with type 1.  
  <https://breakthrought1d.ca/mental-health-support/> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* Mental Health Support (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF))

### Travel `shelf.2`

- **Diabetic supplies** — Canadian Air Transport Security Authority `shelf.2.1`  
  What airport security allows. Insulin, juice and gels can go over 100 mL; declare them to the screening officer.  
  <https://www.catsa-acsta.gc.ca/en/what-can-bring/item/diabetic-supplies> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* Diabetic supplies (Canadian Air Transport Security Authority)
- **Air travel** — Diabetes Canada `shelf.2.2`  
  Insulin in your carry-on, pumps and sensors at screening, and what to pack.  
  <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/life-with-diabetes/the-rights-of-people-living-with-diabetes/air-travel> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* Air Travel (Diabetes Canada)
- **Trips** — Diabetes Québec `shelf.2.3`  
  Planning a trip, and buying travel insurance.  
  <https://www.diabete.qc.ca/en/diabetes/living-with-diabetes/travels/> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* Trips (Diabète Québec)

### Your rights `shelf.3`

- **The rights of people living with diabetes** — Diabetes Canada `shelf.3.1`  
  At work, in public, and in hospital and long-term care.  
  <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/life-with-diabetes/the-rights-of-people-living-with-diabetes> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* The Rights of People Living with Diabetes (Diabetes Canada)
- **Human rights complaints** — Canadian Human Rights Commission `shelf.3.2`  
  For discrimination by a federally regulated employer or service. The Commission also helps you work out where to go instead, such as your province’s or territory’s human rights commission.  
  <https://www.chrc-ccdp.gc.ca/our-work/human-rights-complaints> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* Human rights complaints (Canadian Human Rights Commission)

### Learning about diabetes `shelf.4`

- **Virtual Diabetes Education Program** — Diabetes Canada `shelf.4.1`  
  Free live online sessions led by registered health professionals, for people newly diagnosed or wanting a refresher.  
  <https://www.diabetes.ca/living-with-diabetes/virtual-learning/virtual-diabetes-education-program> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* Virtual Diabetes Education Program (Diabetes Canada)
- **InfoDiabetes Service** — Diabetes Québec `shelf.4.2`  
  Questions about diabetes, answered by Diabetes Québec’s health professionals by phone, email or chat. Not an emergency service: for an emergency, call 911.  
  <https://www.diabete.qc.ca/en/service/infodiabetes-service/> · same tab, an English page  
  *Register:* InfoDiabetes Service (Diabète Québec)

## Closing

**A life, not a list** `closing.heading`

Most of this becomes routine: a look at your feet, some movement most days, a few checkups a year. The rest is knowing who to ask. `closing.body`

## Disclaimer

This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your targets, your medicines and your checkup schedule depend on you. Your team sets them. `disclaimer`

Always link this update: the old /chapter-14 still loads with older guidance (retreat below 4.0; 1 mg glucagon only). Table 4: 150 mL juice or regular soft drink; 6 Life Savers; 15 mL honey.
